questions.q: Which port does SSH use?
questions.why: SSH uses TCP 22. Telnet is 23, FTP control 21 and SMTP 25.

questions.q: Which port does DNS use for standard queries?
questions.why: DNS uses port 53, UDP for most queries and TCP for zone transfers and large replies.

questions.q: Which ports does DHCP use?
questions.why: The DHCP server listens on 67 and clients use 68.

questions.q: Which port does RDP use?
questions.why: Remote Desktop Protocol listens on TCP 3389. 5900 is VNC and 3306 MySQL.

questions.q: Which port does SNMP use for queries?
questions.why: Managers poll agents on 161; agents send traps to managers on 162.

questions.q: Which port does syslog traditionally use?
questions.why: Syslog uses UDP 514; secure syslog over TLS commonly uses TCP 6514.

questions.q: Which port does NTP use?
questions.why: Network Time Protocol uses UDP 123 to synchronise clocks.

questions.q: Which port does SMB use directly over TCP?
questions.why: Modern SMB runs on TCP 445; 137–139 are the older NetBIOS ports.

questions.q: Which port does LDAP use?
questions.why: LDAP uses 389; LDAPS uses 636 and Kerberos uses 88.

questions.q: Which port does IMAP over TLS use?
questions.why: IMAP uses 143 and IMAPS 993. POP3 uses 110 and POP3S 995.

questions.q: Which port does SMTP submission from mail clients usually use?
questions.why: Clients submit mail on 587 with STARTTLS; servers relay to each other on 25.

questions.q: Which port does TFTP use?
questions.why: TFTP is a simple UDP file transfer with no authentication, often used for device images.

questions.q: Which port does SQL Server use by default?
questions.why: Microsoft SQL Server uses 1433. MySQL is 3306, Oracle 1521 and PostgreSQL 5432.

questions.q: Which traffic type sends a packet to every host on the local network?
questions.why: Broadcasts reach all hosts in the broadcast domain, which is why too many can slow a network.

questions.q: Which traffic type is sent to a group of interested receivers?
questions.why: Multicast is efficient for streaming to many receivers who have joined the group.

questions.q: Which IPv4 range is reserved for multicast?
questions.why: Class D, 224.0.0.0/4, is reserved for multicast groups.

questions.q: What does an address in 169.254.0.0/16 on a Windows PC usually mean?
options: It couldn't reach a DHCP server and assigned itself an APIPA address
It is using a static address
questions.why: APIPA lets local communication continue, but the PC won't reach other networks.

questions.q: Which IPv4 address is the loopback address?
questions.why: 127.0.0.0/8 is loopback; traffic to it never leaves the host.

questions.q: Which RFC 1918 range is a single class B-sized block of private addresses?
questions.why: 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255 is the /12 private range.

questions.q: What is the 100.64.0.0/10 range used for?
questions.why: ISPs use it between their NAT devices and customers.

questions.q: How long is an IPv6 address?
questions.why: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hex digits.

questions.q: Which IPv6 address type begins with fe80::?
questions.why: Link-local addresses are created automatically and only work on the local link.

questions.q: Which is the IPv6 loopback address?
questions.why: ::1 is loopback; :: alone means unspecified.

questions.q: What does SLAAC let an IPv6 host do?
options: Configure its own address from the router's advertised prefix
questions.why: Stateless address autoconfiguration needs no DHCP server for the address.

questions.q: Which IPv6 addresses start with fc00::/7 (usually fd)?
questions.why: ULAs are like private IPv4 ranges, routable inside an organisation but not on the internet.
Drop leading zeros in each group and replace one run of zero groups with ::, used once only.

questions.q: What replaced ARP in IPv6?
questions.why: NDP uses ICMPv6 messages to find neighbours' link-layer addresses and routers.

questions.q: What is dual stack?
options: Running IPv4 and IPv6 at the same time on devices
questions.why: Dual stack lets a network move to IPv6 while still supporting IPv4.

questions.q: What is tunnelling in IPv6 transition?
options: Carrying IPv6 packets inside IPv4 across networks that only support IPv4
questions.why: Methods such as 6to4 wrap IPv6 in IPv4 headers.

questions.q: What does NAT do?
options: Translates private internal addresses to public addresses
questions.why: NAT lets many private hosts share public addresses.

questions.q: What is PAT (port address translation)?
options: Many internal hosts share one public IP, distinguished by port numbers
questions.why: PAT, also called NAT overload, is what most home routers do.

questions.q: What is static NAT used for?
options: Sharing one address among many hosts
Mapping one internal address permanently to one public address, such as for a server
questions.why: Static NAT lets outside users reach an internal server at a fixed public address.

questions.q: What is a default route?
options: The route used when no more specific route matches, often 0.0.0.0/0
questions.why: Traffic for unknown destinations goes to the default gateway.

questions.q: When a router has several routes to a destination, which does it choose first?
options: The most specific route (longest prefix match)
The route with the highest metric
questions.why: A /24 route beats a /16 route for an address inside both.

questions.q: What is administrative distance?
options: A rating of how trustworthy a routing source is; lower is preferred
questions.why: When two protocols offer the same route, the one with lower AD wins, such as OSPF over RIP.

questions.q: Which routing protocol is used between organisations on the internet?
questions.why: BGP is the path-vector protocol that exchanges routes between autonomous systems.

questions.q: What metric does OSPF use?
questions.why: Faster links get lower costs, so OSPF prefers higher-bandwidth paths.

questions.q: What is the maximum hop count for RIP?
questions.why: RIP treats 16 as unreachable, which limits it to small networks.

questions.q: What is an OSPF area 0?
options: The backbone area that other areas connect to
questions.why: All OSPF areas must connect to area 0 for routes to pass between them.

questions.q: Which is a link-state protocol?
questions.why: Link-state routers share topology information and each calculates the best paths.

questions.q: What does a first hop redundancy protocol such as VRRP provide?
options: A shared virtual gateway address that moves to a backup router if the main one fails
questions.why: Hosts keep the same default gateway even when a router goes down.

questions.q: What is a virtual IP (VIP)?
options: An address not tied to one physical interface, shared by devices for redundancy or load balancing
questions.why: VIPs are used by FHRPs and load balancers so services stay at one address.

questions.q: What is a subinterface used for in router-on-a-stick?
options: Routing between VLANs over one physical link using 802.1Q tags
questions.why: Each subinterface handles one VLAN on the trunk to the switch.

questions.q: What does 802.1Q define?
questions.why: 802.1Q inserts a tag with the VLAN ID into Ethernet frames on trunks.

questions.q: What is a native VLAN?
options: The VLAN whose traffic crosses a trunk untagged
questions.why: Native VLANs should match on both ends and usually be changed from VLAN 1 for security.

questions.q: What is a voice VLAN?
options: A separate VLAN for IP phones so voice traffic can be prioritised
questions.why: A switch port can carry a PC's data VLAN and the phone's voice VLAN together.

questions.q: What is the difference between an access port and a trunk port?
options: An access port carries one VLAN; a trunk carries many VLANs with tags
questions.why: End devices connect to access ports; switches connect to each other with trunks.

questions.q: What does link aggregation (LACP) do?
options: Combines several physical links into one logical link for bandwidth and redundancy
questions.why: If one member link fails, traffic continues on the others.

questions.q: What does Spanning Tree Protocol select first?
questions.why: The switch with the lowest bridge ID becomes root, and paths are calculated from it.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of Rapid STP (802.1w) over original STP?
options: It removes the need for VLANs
Much faster convergence after topology changes
questions.why: RSTP converges in seconds instead of 30 to 50 seconds.

questions.q: What are jumbo frames?
options: Ethernet frames larger than the standard 1500-byte MTU, often 9000 bytes
questions.why: Jumbo frames reduce overhead for storage traffic, but every device on the path must support them.

questions.q: What happens if a packet is larger than a link's MTU and can't be fragmented?
options: It is dropped, often causing connection problems
questions.why: Path MTU mismatches can make some sites load while large transfers hang.

questions.q: Which 802.11 standard is Wi-Fi 6?
questions.why: Wi-Fi 6 is 802.11ax; Wi-Fi 5 is 802.11ac and Wi-Fi 4 is 802.11n.

questions.q: Which frequency band did Wi-Fi 6E add?
questions.why: 6 GHz offers many more clean channels than 2.4 or 5 GHz.

questions.q: Which 2.4 GHz channels don't overlap in North America?
questions.why: Using only 1, 6 and 11 avoids adjacent-channel interference.

questions.q: What is a benefit of the 5 GHz band over 2.4 GHz?
questions.why: 5 GHz has more non-overlapping channels, but its range is shorter.

questions.q: What is channel bonding in Wi-Fi?
options: Using one channel for all APs
Combining adjacent channels into a wider one for more throughput
questions.why: 40, 80 or 160 MHz channels are faster but use more spectrum and can increase interference.

questions.q: What is the difference between an SSID and a BSSID?
options: The SSID is the network name; the BSSID is the MAC address of a specific AP radio
SSID is the AP's IP address
questions.why: Many APs can share one SSID (an ESS), but each radio has its own BSSID.

questions.q: What is an ESSID?
options: One network name used across multiple APs so clients can roam
questions.why: An extended service set lets users move between APs without changing networks.

questions.q: What is ad hoc wireless mode?
options: Devices connect directly to each other without an AP
APs connect to each other only
questions.why: Infrastructure mode uses APs; ad hoc is peer-to-peer.

questions.q: What is a wireless mesh network?
options: APs connect to each other wirelessly to extend coverage
questions.why: Mesh nodes relay traffic, which helps where running cables is hard.

questions.q: Which antenna type sends signal in all horizontal directions?
questions.why: Omnidirectional antennas suit open offices; directional antennas focus signal one way.

questions.q: Which antenna type is best for a point-to-point link between buildings?
questions.why: Focusing energy in one direction increases range and reduces interference.

questions.q: Which wireless security is strongest for a home network?
questions.why: WPA3-Personal uses SAE, which resists offline password cracking.

questions.q: What is a captive portal?
options: A web page users must use to log in or accept terms before getting network access
questions.why: Hotels and guest networks commonly use captive portals.

questions.q: What is a wireless LAN controller?
options: A device that centrally manages many access points
questions.why: Controllers push configuration, manage roaming and monitor all APs from one place.

questions.q: What does a site survey determine?
options: Where APs should go and what coverage and interference exist
questions.why: Surveys produce heat maps showing signal strength across the area.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a patch panel?
options: Terminating cable runs in one place so connections can be changed with patch cables
questions.why: Patch panels keep cabling organised and make moves and changes easy.

questions.q: What is a 110 block used for?
options: Terminating twisted-pair cable, often for telephone and data
questions.why: Wires are punched down into a 110 block with a punch-down tool.

questions.q: What is an SFP module?
options: A hot-swappable transceiver that lets a switch port use fiber or copper
questions.why: Small form-factor pluggables let you choose the media and distance per port.

questions.q: What does a fiber connector type LC look like compared with SC?
options: LC is a small, latching connector; SC is larger and square with push-pull
LC is threaded; SC is a bayonet
questions.why: LC's small size suits high-density panels.

questions.q: What is the main difference between UPC and APC fiber connectors?
options: APC has an angled end face that reduces back reflection
questions.why: APC connectors are usually green; UPC are usually blue. Mixing them causes loss.

questions.q: What is PoE used for?
options: Delivering power to devices like phones, cameras and APs over Ethernet cable
questions.why: PoE removes the need for separate power cables at each device.

questions.q: How much power can 802.3at (PoE+) supply per port?
questions.why: 802.3af gives 15.4 W, 802.3at 30 W and 802.3bt up to 60 or 90 W.

questions.q: Why are servers mounted in racks measured in U?
options: U is the number of ports
One rack unit is 1.75 inches of vertical space
questions.why: A 2U server takes 3.5 inches of rack height.

questions.q: What is hot aisle/cold aisle?
options: Arranging racks so cool air enters fronts and hot exhaust is collected from the backs
questions.why: It stops hot and cold air mixing and improves cooling efficiency.

questions.q: Why monitor humidity in a server room?
options: Too low causes static discharge; too high causes condensation
questions.why: Keeping humidity in range protects equipment.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a physical network diagram?
options: Showing where devices and cables are physically located
questions.why: Logical diagrams show addressing and flows; physical diagrams show real locations.

questions.q: What is a logical network diagram?
options: A floor plan of cable runs
A diagram showing IP subnets, VLANs and how traffic flows
questions.why: Logical diagrams help with troubleshooting routing and segmentation.

questions.q: What is an IDF?
options: An intermediate distribution frame, a wiring closet serving part of a building
questions.why: IDFs connect back to the main distribution frame (MDF).

questions.q: What does a baseline help network administrators do?
options: Spot abnormal performance by comparing with normal behaviour
questions.why: If utilisation is far above baseline, something has changed.

questions.q: What is an SNMP MIB?
options: A database describing the objects a device can report
questions.why: Managers use MIB object IDs (OIDs) to query values like interface counters.

questions.q: What is an SNMP trap?
options: An unsolicited alert sent from a device to the manager
questions.why: Traps tell the manager about events like a link going down.

questions.q: Which SNMP version supports authentication and encryption?
questions.why: v1 and v2c use plain-text community strings.

questions.q: What is port mirroring (SPAN)?
options: Assigning a port to a VLAN
Copying a port's traffic to another port for analysis
questions.why: A packet analyser on the mirror port can see the traffic without being in line.

questions.q: What is a network tap?
options: A hardware device that copies traffic passing through a link
questions.why: Taps give a complete copy of traffic, including errors, without depending on switch resources.

questions.q: What does a packet capture show that NetFlow doesn't?
questions.why: Flows are summaries; captures show the full packets.

questions.q: What is jitter?
questions.why: High jitter causes choppy voice and video, which jitter buffers try to smooth.

questions.q: What is latency?
options: The amount of data per second
The time it takes data to travel from source to destination
questions.why: High latency makes interactive applications feel slow.

questions.q: What is the difference between bandwidth and throughput?
options: Bandwidth is the maximum capacity; throughput is the actual data rate achieved
questions.why: Overhead, congestion and errors make throughput lower than bandwidth.

questions.q: What does QoS DSCP marking do?
options: Labels packets with a priority so devices can treat them differently
questions.why: Voice is often marked EF so it gets priority queuing.

questions.q: What is a DHCP reservation?
options: A fixed address always given to a specific device's MAC address
questions.why: Reservations give consistent addresses to printers or servers while still using DHCP.

questions.q: What is a DHCP scope?
options: The range of addresses and settings a DHCP server hands out for a subnet
questions.why: Scopes include the address pool, mask, gateway and DNS options.

questions.q: What does a DHCP lease time control?
options: How long a client may use an address before renewing
How long the server stays up
questions.why: Short leases suit busy guest networks; long leases suit stable office networks.

questions.q: Why would you configure a DHCP relay (IP helper)?
options: To forward DHCP broadcasts from one subnet to a server on another
questions.why: Broadcasts don't cross routers, so the relay forwards them to the central server.

questions.q: Which DNS record maps a name to an IPv4 address?
questions.why: A records map a name to IPv4; AAAA records map to IPv6.

questions.q: Which DNS record gives an alias pointing to another name?
questions.why: For example, www can be a CNAME for the main host name.

questions.q: Which DNS record identifies a domain's mail servers?
questions.why: MX records list mail servers with priorities.

questions.q: Which DNS record is used for reverse lookups?
questions.why: PTR records map an IP address back to a name.

questions.q: Which DNS record holds text such as SPF policies?
questions.why: TXT records store SPF, DKIM keys and domain verification strings.

questions.q: Which DNS record lists the authoritative name servers for a zone?
questions.why: NS records delegate a zone to its authoritative servers.

questions.q: What is the SOA record?
options: The start of authority record with zone details such as serial number and timers
questions.why: Secondary servers check the SOA serial to know when to transfer the zone.

questions.q: What does an SRV record do?
options: Identifies the host and port for a specific service
questions.why: Services like SIP and Active Directory use SRV records to find servers.

questions.q: What is DNS TTL?
options: How long a record may be cached before it must be looked up again
questions.why: Lower TTLs make changes take effect faster but increase query load.

questions.q: What is the difference between a recursive and an iterative DNS query?
options: Recursive asks the server to find the full answer; iterative gets referrals to follow
questions.why: Clients usually ask a resolver recursively; resolvers query root and TLD servers iteratively.

questions.q: What is an authoritative DNS server?
options: A server that holds the original records for a zone
questions.why: Authoritative answers come from the zone's own servers, not a cache.

questions.q: What is PTP used for?
options: Very precise clock synchronisation, more accurate than NTP
questions.why: Precision Time Protocol is used where microsecond accuracy matters.

questions.q: What is an NTP stratum?
options: A level showing distance from the reference clock; stratum 1 is closest
questions.why: Stratum 0 is the reference clock, stratum 1 servers connect to it directly, and so on.

questions.q: What is out-of-band management?
options: Managing devices through a separate network or connection from production traffic
Managing devices through the normal network
questions.why: If the production network fails, out-of-band access still works.

questions.q: What is a console connection used for?
options: Direct local configuration of a network device through its console port
questions.why: Console access works even when the device has no network configuration.

questions.q: Why use SSH instead of Telnet to manage switches?
options: SSH encrypts the session, including passwords
questions.why: Telnet sends everything, passwords included, in clear text.

questions.q: What is a site-to-site VPN?
options: A VPN connecting two networks, such as offices, through gateways
A VPN for one remote user
questions.why: Users at each site don't need VPN software; the gateways handle the tunnel.

questions.q: What is a full tunnel VPN?
options: All client traffic, including internet traffic, goes through the VPN
Only corporate traffic uses the VPN
questions.why: Full tunnels let the company inspect all traffic but add load and latency.

questions.q: What is an API used for in network management?
options: Letting software configure and query devices programmatically
questions.why: APIs support automation tools and controllers.

questions.q: What is a VXLAN used for?
options: Extending layer 2 networks across a layer 3 network
questions.why: VXLAN encapsulates frames in UDP, allowing millions of segments in data centres.

questions.q: What is zero trust architecture in networking?
options: Every access request is verified regardless of network location
questions.why: Being inside the network doesn't grant trust by itself.

questions.q: What is a VPC in cloud networking?
options: A virtual private cloud, an isolated network for your cloud resources
questions.why: VPCs have their own subnets, routing and security controls.

questions.q: What is a cloud internet gateway used for?
options: Allowing resources in a VPC to reach the internet
questions.why: Public subnets route to the internet gateway; private subnets usually use NAT.

questions.q: What is a NAT gateway in the cloud?
options: Lets instances in private subnets reach the internet without being reachable from it
Lets the internet reach private instances
questions.why: Outbound updates work while inbound connections are blocked.

questions.q: What is VPC peering?
options: Connecting two VPCs so they can communicate privately
Connecting a VPC to the internet
questions.why: Peered VPCs route traffic between them without going over the internet.

questions.q: What is a network security group (or security list) in the cloud?
options: Rules that allow or deny traffic to cloud resources
questions.why: They act as virtual firewalls at the subnet or instance level.

questions.q: What is cloud elasticity?
options: Automatically adding or removing resources as demand changes
questions.why: Elasticity lets you pay for what you use and handle spikes.

questions.q: What is multitenancy in the cloud?
options: Multiple customers sharing the same physical infrastructure, logically separated
questions.why: Isolation between tenants is a key security responsibility for providers.

questions.q: What does a direct cloud connection (like Direct Connect or ExpressRoute) provide?
options: A private, dedicated link from your network to the cloud provider
questions.why: Private links give more consistent performance than VPNs over the internet.

questions.q: What is a content delivery network (CDN)?
options: Servers around the world that cache content close to users
questions.why: CDNs reduce latency and absorb traffic spikes.

questions.q: What is the first step of the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology?
questions.why: Gather information, question users, identify symptoms and determine what changed.

questions.q: During troubleshooting, what should you do if your theory is not confirmed?
options: Establish a new theory or escalate
questions.why: Unconfirmed theories mean going back to step 2 or asking for help.

questions.q: What does 'question the obvious' mean in troubleshooting?
options: Check simple causes first, such as cables and power
questions.why: Many problems turn out to be unplugged cables or switched-off devices.

questions.q: Which tool checks which wires in a cable are connected correctly?
questions.why: Cable testers find opens, shorts and miswires.

questions.q: Which tool finds a specific cable among many in a bundle or wall?
questions.why: The toner sends a signal down the cable and the probe detects it at the other end.

questions.q: Which tool measures signal loss and locates faults on fiber?
questions.why: An optical time-domain reflectometer shows the distance to breaks and bad splices.

questions.q: What does a Wi-Fi analyser show?
options: Nearby networks, channels, signal strength and interference
questions.why: It helps choose less crowded channels and spot rogue APs.

questions.q: Which tool shows radio interference from non-Wi-Fi sources such as microwaves?
questions.why: Spectrum analysers see all RF energy, not just Wi-Fi frames.

questions.q: What is a loopback plug used for?
options: Testing a network port by sending its signal back to itself
questions.why: If the port works with the loopback, the problem is elsewhere.

questions.q: Which command shows the path packets take to a destination on Windows?
questions.why: tracert lists each router hop and its response time.

questions.q: Which command shows a Windows host's IP configuration including DNS servers?
questions.why: /all adds MAC address, DHCP and DNS details.

questions.q: Which command releases and renews a DHCP address on Windows?
questions.why: Releasing and renewing gets a fresh lease from the DHCP server.

questions.q: Which command clears the DNS cache on Windows?
questions.why: Flushing the cache forces new lookups, which helps after DNS changes.

questions.q: Which command shows listening ports and active connections?
questions.why: netstat -an lists every connection and listening port.

questions.q: Which command queries DNS servers directly to test name resolution?
questions.why: These tools show exactly which records a DNS server returns.

questions.q: Which Linux command shows network interfaces and addresses?
questions.why: ip addr (or ifconfig on older systems) lists interfaces and addresses.

questions.q: Which command shows the MAC addresses a host has learned for local IPs?
questions.why: arp -a shows the ARP cache of IP-to-MAC mappings.

questions.q: Which command on a Cisco switch shows the MAC address table?
questions.why: It lists which MAC addresses are on which ports and VLANs.

questions.q: Which Cisco command shows interface status and errors?
questions.why: It shows up/down status, speed, duplex and error counters such as CRC errors.

questions.q: Users report slow speeds and a switch interface shows many CRC errors. What is the most likely cause?
options: A damaged cable or bad connector
questions.why: CRC errors mean frames arrive corrupted, which almost always points to physical layer problems.

questions.q: One side of a link is set to full duplex and the other to half duplex. What symptom appears?
questions.why: Duplex mismatches cause collisions on the half-duplex side and slow, unreliable transfers.

questions.q: A cable run of 120 metres of Cat 6 gives an unreliable connection. Why?
options: The switch needs a firmware update
It exceeds the 100-metre limit for twisted-pair Ethernet
questions.why: Signal attenuation beyond 100 metres causes errors; use fiber or add a switch in between.

questions.q: What is crosstalk?
options: Signal from one wire pair interfering with another
Two users talking on one phone
questions.why: Untwisting too much of a pair at the connector increases crosstalk.

questions.q: What causes attenuation in a cable?
questions.why: All media lose strength over distance, which is why each has a maximum length.

questions.q: A newly installed fiber link shows no light at the far end. What should be checked first?
options: Whether transmit and receive strands are swapped
questions.why: A TX/RX reversal is one of the most common fiber installation mistakes.

questions.q: What is a dirty fiber connector likely to cause?
options: High signal loss and link errors
questions.why: Dust on the end face blocks light; connectors should be cleaned and inspected before use.

questions.q: Which problem occurs when single-mode and multimode fiber are mixed on one link?
options: Excessive signal loss due to a core size mismatch
questions.why: The different core diameters don't match, so much of the light is lost.

questions.q: A switch port's LED is amber or off after connecting a PC. What does this suggest?
options: A physical link problem or a disabled port
questions.why: Link lights show layer 1 status; no link means checking the cable, port and NIC.

questions.q: Two devices on a network have the same IP address. What symptom appears?
options: Intermittent connectivity for one or both devices
questions.why: Each device keeps claiming the address in ARP, so traffic goes to whichever answered last.

questions.q: Users can reach websites by IP address but not by name. What is the likely cause?
questions.why: If IP connectivity works but names fail, name resolution is the broken piece.

questions.q: A PC can reach local devices but not the internet. What should be checked first?
questions.why: Traffic for other networks goes to the default gateway; a wrong or missing one blocks it.

questions.q: A user has a 169.254.x.x address. What is the most likely problem?
options: The PC couldn't get an address from DHCP
The PC has a static IP
questions.why: APIPA addresses mean DHCP failed, so check the DHCP server, scope and connectivity.

questions.q: The DHCP scope has run out of addresses. What is the symptom?
options: New devices can't get an address
questions.why: Shorter leases, a larger scope or cleaning up stale leases fixes exhaustion.

questions.q: A rogue DHCP server is on the network. What will clients experience?
options: Wrong IP settings such as an incorrect gateway, breaking connectivity
questions.why: DHCP snooping on switches stops untrusted ports from answering DHCP requests.

questions.q: After a VLAN change, a PC can't reach its usual servers. What is the likely cause?
options: The port is in the wrong VLAN
questions.why: A port in the wrong VLAN puts the PC on a different subnet from its servers.

questions.q: What is a broadcast storm?
options: Broadcasts multiplying endlessly, often due to a switching loop
questions.why: Loops make broadcasts circle forever and can bring a network down; STP prevents this.

questions.q: Why might a routing loop occur?
options: Routers have inconsistent routes that send packets back and forth
questions.why: TTL eventually discards looping packets, but performance suffers until routes converge.

questions.q: What does an asymmetric route problem mean?
options: Traffic goes out one path and returns another, which can break stateful firewalls
questions.why: A firewall that only sees one direction of a session may drop the return traffic.

questions.q: Users on one floor have weak Wi-Fi. What is the likely cause?
options: Too few access points or obstacles blocking signal
questions.why: Walls, floors and distance weaken signals; a site survey shows where APs are needed.

questions.q: Many APs use the same 2.4 GHz channel in an office. What problem results?
questions.why: APs on the same channel share airtime, so planning channels 1, 6 and 11 helps.

questions.q: A laptop shows full Wi-Fi signal but very slow speed. What could be the cause?
questions.why: Signal strength isn't everything; noise and contention reduce throughput.

questions.q: What is RSSI in wireless?
options: A measure of received signal strength
questions.why: Values closer to 0 dBm are stronger; -67 dBm is a common target for good performance.

questions.q: What is the effect of an AP's transmit power being set too high?
options: Clients may stick to a distant AP instead of roaming to a nearer one
questions.why: Power that's too high also increases interference with neighbouring APs.

questions.q: What is a client 'sticking' to an AP called?
questions.why: The device keeps a weak connection instead of roaming, causing poor performance.

questions.q: Clients fail to connect after an AP was changed to WPA3 only. Why might this happen?
questions.why: WPA3 transition mode supports both WPA2 and WPA3 clients during migration.

questions.q: What is the likely cause if wireless clients connect but can't get past a captive portal?
options: The portal or authentication service is failing
The channel width is too narrow
The DNS TTL is too long
questions.why: Clients associate to Wi-Fi but stay restricted until the portal authenticates them.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a network change management process?
options: Ensuring changes are reviewed, approved, tested and documented
questions.why: Uncontrolled changes are a leading cause of outages.

questions.q: What is configuration management for network devices?
options: Tracking and controlling device configurations and versions
questions.why: Saved configurations make it easy to restore or compare after problems.

questions.q: Why back up network device configurations?
options: To restore quickly after failure or a bad change
questions.why: A replacement switch can be restored from the saved configuration in minutes.

questions.q: What is the difference between running-config and startup-config on a Cisco device?
options: Running is active in memory; startup loads at boot
Running is on the console only
questions.why: Changes are lost at reboot unless the running config is saved to startup.

questions.q: What is asset lifecycle management?
options: Managing devices from purchase through support to disposal
questions.why: Knowing when devices reach end of support avoids running unpatched equipment.

questions.q: What does end-of-support mean for a network device?
options: The vendor no longer provides updates or help
questions.why: Unsupported devices get no security fixes and should be replaced.

questions.q: What is an SLA in network services?
options: An agreement defining service levels, such as uptime, with a provider
questions.why: SLAs set expectations and remedies when providers miss targets.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a standard operating procedure (SOP)?
options: Documented steps so tasks are done consistently
questions.why: SOPs reduce errors and help new staff work correctly.

questions.q: What does an IP address management (IPAM) system track?
options: IP address allocations, subnets and usage
questions.why: IPAM prevents conflicts and shows which addresses are free.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a network access control list (ACL) on a router?
options: Permitting or denying traffic based on rules
questions.why: ACLs filter by address, protocol and port.

questions.q: What is implicit deny in an ACL?
options: Traffic not explicitly permitted is blocked by default
questions.why: Every ACL ends with an invisible deny-all rule.

questions.q: Why does the order of ACL rules matter?
options: Rules are processed top to bottom and the first match wins
questions.why: A broad permit above a specific deny would let the traffic through.

questions.q: What is a screened subnet used for in network design?
options: Hosting public-facing servers separated from the internal network
questions.why: Firewalls control traffic between the internet, the screened subnet and the internal network.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a guest network?
options: Giving visitors internet access while keeping them off internal systems
questions.why: Guest networks are isolated, often with a captive portal and bandwidth limits.

questions.q: What is defence in depth?
options: Using several layers of security controls
questions.why: If one control fails, others still protect the network.

questions.q: What is an IoT security concern on corporate networks?
options: Devices often have weak security and should be segmented
questions.why: Putting IoT devices on their own VLAN limits damage if one is compromised.

questions.q: What is MAC spoofing?
options: Changing a device's MAC address to impersonate another
questions.why: Spoofing can bypass MAC filters, which is why they're weak on their own.

questions.q: What is VLAN hopping?
options: Gaining access to traffic on another VLAN, such as through switch spoofing or double tagging
Moving a port to a new VLAN legitimately
questions.why: Disabling auto-trunking and changing the native VLAN prevent it.

questions.q: How do you prevent switch spoofing VLAN hopping attacks?
options: Disable dynamic trunking negotiation on access ports
questions.why: Access ports should be fixed as access, so a device can't negotiate a trunk.

questions.q: What is DNS poisoning?
options: Inserting false DNS records so users go to malicious sites
questions.why: DNSSEC and secure resolvers help prevent it.

questions.q: What is an on-path attack in networking?
options: An attacker intercepting traffic between two parties
questions.why: ARP poisoning and evil twin APs are common ways to get on-path.

questions.q: What is a deauthentication attack?
options: Forcing wireless clients to disconnect using forged management frames
questions.why: 802.11w protected management frames defend against it.

questions.q: What is a rogue access point?
options: An AP on the wrong channel
An unauthorised AP connected to the network
questions.why: Rogue APs bypass security; wireless IDS and NAC help find them.

questions.q: What is DHCP snooping?
options: A switch feature that blocks DHCP replies from untrusted ports
questions.why: Only ports leading to real DHCP servers are trusted, stopping rogue servers.

questions.q: What is dynamic ARP inspection?
options: Validating ARP packets against trusted bindings to stop ARP spoofing
questions.why: DAI uses the DHCP snooping table to drop forged ARP replies.

questions.q: What is the purpose of BPDU guard?
options: Shutting a port that receives STP messages where only end devices should be
questions.why: It stops someone plugging in a switch that could disrupt the spanning tree.

questions.q: What is the purpose of root guard?
options: Preventing another switch from becoming the STP root bridge on that port
questions.why: It keeps the intended root bridge in place.

questions.q: What is a DDoS attack?
options: Many systems flooding a target to make it unavailable
questions.why: Botnets generate massive traffic; providers and scrubbing services help absorb it.

questions.q: Which control best protects management interfaces of network devices?
options: Restricting access to a management VLAN and using SSH with strong authentication
questions.why: Isolated management networks and encrypted protocols limit who can reach devices.

questions.q: What does AAA with TACACS+ provide for network devices?
options: Centralised authentication, authorisation and accounting for admin access
questions.why: TACACS+ encrypts the whole payload and separates authorisation, suiting device administration.

questions.q: What is the difference between RADIUS and TACACS+?
options: RADIUS combines authentication and authorisation and is common for network access; TACACS+ separates them and suits device admin
questions.why: RADIUS encrypts only the password; TACACS+ encrypts the entire payload.

questions.q: What is geofencing as a network control?
options: A fence around the server room
Allowing or blocking access based on location
questions.why: Access might be blocked from countries where the company doesn't operate.

questions.q: What is a honeypot used for in network security?
options: Luring attackers to detect and study them
questions.why: No legitimate traffic should reach a honeypot, so any connection is suspicious.

questions.q: What is the main difference between an IDS and an IPS?
options: An IPS can block traffic inline; an IDS only alerts
An IDS blocks; an IPS alerts
questions.why: IPS sits in the traffic path, so false positives can block legitimate traffic.

questions.q: What is a signature-based IDS?
options: Detection that matches traffic against known attack patterns
questions.why: Signatures catch known attacks but miss new ones.

questions.q: What is anomaly-based detection?
options: Flagging traffic that differs from a learned normal baseline
questions.why: It can catch new attacks but may produce more false positives.

questions.q: What is the purpose of disaster recovery testing?
options: Proving that recovery plans actually work before a real disaster
questions.why: Untested plans often fail when they're really needed.

questions.q: What does RPO measure in network disaster recovery?
options: The maximum acceptable data loss measured in time
questions.why: An RPO of one hour means backups or replication must happen at least hourly.

questions.q: What is MTTR?
options: Mean time to repair or recover after a failure
questions.why: Lower MTTR means services come back faster.

questions.q: What is a hot site in network disaster recovery?
options: A site with hardware but no data
A fully equipped site with current data, ready to take over almost immediately
questions.why: Hot sites are the most expensive but give the fastest recovery.

questions.q: What is active-active redundancy?
options: All redundant systems handle traffic at the same time
questions.why: Active-active uses all capacity and keeps working if one fails.

questions.q: What is active-passive redundancy?
options: A standby system takes over only if the active one fails
questions.why: The passive unit sits idle until needed.

questions.q: What is a WAN?
options: A network connecting sites over a large geographic area
questions.why: WAN links connect offices across cities or countries.

questions.q: What is MPLS?
options: A provider WAN technology that forwards traffic using labels
questions.why: MPLS offers predictable performance and supports traffic classes.

questions.q: What is a leased line?
options: A dedicated point-to-point circuit rented from a provider
questions.why: Leased lines give dedicated, consistent bandwidth.

questions.q: What is DSL?
questions.why: Speed drops with distance from the provider's equipment.

questions.q: What is the main drawback of satellite internet for real-time apps?
questions.why: Geostationary satellite links add hundreds of milliseconds of delay; low-earth-orbit systems are better.

questions.q: What is 5G's main benefit for business connectivity?
options: High speeds and low latency over cellular networks
questions.why: 5G can serve as a primary or backup WAN link.

questions.q: What is a demarc point?
options: Where the service provider's responsibility ends and the customer's begins
questions.why: Troubleshooting often starts by checking whether a fault is before or after the demarc.

questions.q: What is a smart jack?
options: A provider device at the demarc that allows remote testing of the line
questions.why: The carrier can loop the line back from the smart jack to test it.

questions.q: What does a network load balancer use to decide where to send traffic?
options: Algorithms such as round-robin or least connections
questions.why: Health checks also stop traffic going to failed servers.

questions.q: What does a proxy server do for web traffic?
options: Makes requests on behalf of clients and can filter and cache them
questions.why: Proxies log browsing and block unwanted sites.

questions.q: What is a VPN concentrator?
options: A device that handles many VPN connections at once
questions.why: Concentrators terminate large numbers of remote access tunnels.

questions.q: What is a layer 3 switch?
options: A switch that can also route between VLANs
questions.why: Layer 3 switches route at hardware speed inside a campus network.

questions.q: What is a unified threat management (UTM) appliance?
options: A single device combining firewall, IPS, antivirus and filtering
questions.why: UTMs simplify small networks but can become a single point of failure.

questions.q: What is network function virtualisation (NFV)?
options: Running network functions like firewalls and routers as software on standard servers
questions.why: NFV replaces dedicated appliances with virtual ones that can be deployed quickly.

questions.q: What is a storage area network (SAN)?
options: A dedicated network giving servers block-level access to shared storage
questions.why: SANs use protocols such as Fibre Channel or iSCSI.

questions.q: What is iSCSI?
options: A protocol carrying SCSI storage commands over IP networks
questions.why: iSCSI lets ordinary Ethernet networks carry SAN traffic.

questions.q: What is NAS?
options: File-level storage accessed over the network by protocols like SMB or NFS
questions.why: Network attached storage serves files; SANs serve blocks.

questions.q: What is the difference between a hub and a switch?
options: A switch repeats to all ports
A hub repeats to all ports; a switch forwards frames only to the destination port
questions.why: Switches reduce collisions and improve security by not flooding all traffic.

questions.q: What is a bridge?
options: A device that connects two network segments and filters traffic by MAC address
questions.why: Bridges were the predecessors of switches.

questions.q: What is a repeater?
options: A device that regenerates a signal to extend distance
questions.why: Repeaters work at layer 1 and don't read addresses.

questions.q: What is a media converter?
options: A device that connects different media, such as fiber to copper
questions.why: Media converters extend links where copper distance limits are exceeded.

questions.q: What layer does a router operate at?
questions.why: Routers forward packets between networks using IP addresses.

questions.q: What layer does a traditional switch operate at?
questions.why: Switches forward frames based on MAC addresses.

questions.q: What does the Transport layer provide?
options: End-to-end delivery, ports, and with TCP, reliability
questions.why: TCP and UDP work at layer 4, using port numbers to reach applications.

questions.q: Which OSI layer manages sessions between applications?
questions.why: Layer 5 sets up, maintains and ends sessions.

questions.q: What does TCP's three-way handshake establish?
options: A reliable connection between two hosts
questions.why: SYN, SYN/ACK and ACK set up sequence numbers before data flows.

questions.q: What does a TCP RST flag do?
options: Immediately resets and ends a connection
questions.why: A RST in reply to a SYN means the port is closed.

questions.q: What is the purpose of TCP windowing?
options: Controlling how much data can be sent before an acknowledgment
questions.why: The window size adapts to network conditions and the receiver's capacity.

questions.q: What is ICMP used for?
options: Network diagnostics and error messages, such as ping and unreachable messages
questions.why: Blocking all ICMP can break path MTU discovery and troubleshooting.

questions.q: What is GRE?
options: A tunnelling protocol that encapsulates packets, often without encryption
questions.why: GRE is often paired with IPsec when encryption is needed.

questions.q: What does IPsec's ESP protocol provide?
options: Encryption, integrity and authentication of packets
questions.why: AH provides integrity without encryption; ESP adds confidentiality.

questions.q: What is the difference between IPsec transport and tunnel mode?
options: Transport protects the payload; tunnel encapsulates the entire original packet
questions.why: Site-to-site VPNs use tunnel mode, which hides the original IP headers.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of HTTPS?
questions.why: TLS protects confidentiality and integrity, and certificates authenticate the server.

questions.q: What is SIP used for?
options: Setting up and managing VoIP calls
questions.why: SIP signals call setup; RTP carries the audio.

questions.q: What is RTP used for?
options: Carrying real-time audio and video streams
questions.why: RTP runs over UDP because retransmitting late voice packets is pointless.

questions.q: Why does VoIP use UDP rather than TCP for voice?
options: Low latency matters more than retransmitting lost packets
questions.why: A retransmitted voice packet would arrive too late to be useful.

questions.q: What does a network baseline report typically include?
options: Normal utilisation, latency and error levels over time
questions.why: Comparing against the baseline reveals unusual activity or growing demand.

questions.q: What are interface errors such as runts and giants?
options: Frames that are too small or too large, often from collisions or misconfiguration
questions.why: Runts often come from collisions; giants from MTU mismatches.

questions.q: What does 'input errors' on an interface usually indicate?
options: Physical problems such as bad cabling or interference
questions.why: Rising input errors point to layer 1 or 2 problems.

questions.q: What is interface discard counting?
options: Frames dropped, often due to congestion or full buffers
questions.why: Many discards suggest the link is overloaded.

questions.q: What is log aggregation?
options: Collecting logs from many devices into one central system
questions.why: Central logs make correlation and searching much easier.

questions.q: What is the purpose of syslog severity levels?
options: Ranking messages from emergency (0) to debug (7)
questions.why: Lower numbers are more severe; filters can forward only important messages.

questions.q: What does a network performance monitoring tool alert on?
options: Thresholds such as high utilisation, latency or device downtime
questions.why: Alerts let teams respond before users notice problems.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a network topology map tool?
options: Automatically discovering and drawing how devices connect
questions.why: Discovery tools use protocols like LLDP, CDP and SNMP.

questions.q: What does LLDP do?
options: Lets network devices advertise their identity and capabilities to neighbours
questions.why: LLDP is vendor-neutral; CDP is Cisco's equivalent.

questions.q: Why might you disable CDP or LLDP on ports facing untrusted devices?
options: They reveal device details that help attackers
questions.why: Model, software version and IP information can help an attacker plan.

questions.q: What is a PDU in networking?
options: The unit of data at each layer, such as frame, packet or segment
questions.why: PDU can also mean the power strip in a rack; context matters.

questions.q: What does a rack PDU provide?
options: Distributing power to equipment in a rack
questions.why: Managed PDUs can report power use and switch outlets remotely.

questions.q: What is a surge protector's role?
questions.why: Surges from lightning or the grid can damage electronics.

questions.q: What does a fire suppression system for a data centre often use?
options: Clean agent gas that doesn't damage electronics
questions.why: Gas systems put out fires without the water damage sprinklers cause.

questions.q: What is the purpose of cable management?
options: Keeping cables organised for airflow, safety and easy troubleshooting
questions.why: Messy cabling blocks airflow and makes changes risky.

questions.q: What is a structured cabling system?
options: A standardised approach to building cabling with patch panels and labelled runs
questions.why: Standards such as TIA-568 define how cabling is installed and labelled.

questions.q: Why label both ends of every cable?
options: To make tracing and troubleshooting faster
questions.why: Labels save time and prevent unplugging the wrong cable.
